info.title: Biohub Officiel V6
info.description:
# Biohub Cell Tracking — 3D+Time Cell Detection & Lineage Reconstruction

## Overview
A CPU-optimized pipeline for detecting and tracking zebrafish embryo cells 
across 3D+time fluorescence microscopy volumes, including division (mitosis) 
event detection for full lineage reconstruction.

## Pipeline Architecture

**1. Detection** — Per-frame cell centroid detection via anisotropy-aware 
Gaussian smoothing + local maxima extraction, with percentile-based 
normalization for noise robustness.

**2. Linking** — Frame-to-frame association using the Hungarian algorithm 
(Linear Assignment Problem) on physically-scaled Euclidean distances 
(z=1.625µm, y=x=0.40625µm/voxel).

**3. Gap Closing** — Recovers tracks interrupted by a single missed 
detection by searching two frames ahead.

**4. Division Detection** — Identifies mitosis events via geometric 
constraints: daughter cell symmetry, inter-daughter distance, and 
trajectory angle divergence.

## Key Engineering Decisions
- Zarr v3 array accessed at canonical path `0/`, shape `(T, Z, Y, X)`
- Single-chunk-per-timepoint reads avoid loading full volumes into memory
- All thresholds tuned for CPU-only execution within Kaggle's 12h limit

## Version Log
- v6: Aligned with official data spec (zarr v3, path `0/`); fixed gap-closing 
  indexing bug; added trajectory-angle filter to reduce false-positive divisions

info.subtitle: Official competition metric + scripts, for offline kernels
info.description:
An **unmodified copy of the official Biohub cell-tracking competition code**
(`royerlab/kaggle-cell-tracking-competition`), packaged as a Kaggle dataset so that
**no-internet kernels** can import it. All credit to the competition organisers; this
is a redistribution for convenience, not original work.

## Why you might want this

Competition kernels run without internet, so you cannot `pip install` or `git clone`
the official package. Attaching this dataset lets you:

- **Score a submission offline with the official metric before spending a daily
  submission slot** - the repo ships `scripts/csv_to_geffs.py` and
  `scripts/evaluate.py`, which together implement the round trip the organisers
  document: predict -> geffs -> CSV -> geffs -> score. No images are loaded.
- Read the exact metric implementation rather than a paraphrase of it.
- Reuse the official training and prediction scripts.

## Important: this is the PATCHED metric

Pinned at commit `075fc5f5a52d11077f9dc2b074644618f26939e2`, which includes
`aa65e90` *"updating metric to patch weakly connected component exploit"*
(2026-07-17).

Some widely used support packs vendor an **older copy** of this code that predates
that patch and still contains `_weakly_connected_components`. If you score locally
with one of those, your division numbers are computed with the pre-patch metric.
A one-line check:

```python
import inspect, tracking_cellmot.division_metrics as dm
assert "_weakly_connected_components" not in inspect.getsource(dm)
```

For reference, the patch changed `division_metrics.py` from 450 to 574 lines
(division scoring substantially rewritten) and 90 lines of `metrics.py`. The
edge-side changes - non-consecutive-edge filtering and duplicate-edge dedup - are
no-ops for graphs that already use consecutive-frame edges with in-degree 1, so if
that describes your output, only your **division** numbers change.

## Caveat on local scoring

Train labels are sparse: annotated edges cover a small fraction of cells, and the
metric ignores edges whose endpoints match no annotated node. A local score is a
useful diagnostic and a good way to catch invalid graphs, but it is **not** a
reliable predictor of leaderboard rank - in our own testing the local ranking of
two pipelines came out inverted relative to the public leaderboard. Treat it
accordingly.

## Contents

- `tracking_cellmot_075fc5f/src/tracking_cellmot/` - the package (`metrics.py`,
  `division_metrics.py`, `io.py`, `img_proc.py`, `models/`)
- `tracking_cellmot_075fc5f/scripts/` - `evaluate.py`, `csv_to_geffs.py`,
  `geffs_to_csv.py`, `train_unet_transformer.py`, `predict_unet_transformer.py`
- `metrics.md` - the organisers' description of the metric
- `USAGE.md` - copy-paste snippets, including how to verify the patched version
  loaded and the `GraphView.detach()` gotcha
- `PROVENANCE.md`, `LICENSE`, `README.md`

## Licence and attribution

BSD 3-Clause, Copyright (c) 2026 Thibaut Goldsborough. Source:
<https://github.com/royerlab/kaggle-cell-tracking-competition>

**Check upstream for newer commits.** This is a pinned snapshot; if the organisers
patch the metric again, this dataset will be stale until it is re-versioned.

info.title: Biohub Local Scoring Support Pack
info.subtitle: Score your cell tracker on train with the exact competition metric, on CPU
info.description:
# Biohub Local Scoring Support Pack

The [biohub cell-tracking competition](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/biohub-cell-tracking-during-development) scores a node-and-edge lineage graph with a custom edge-and-division metric, and there is no way to know your number without spending a submission. This pack fixes that: a drop-in `local_score(submission, gt_dir)` that wraps the organisers' OWN scoring code, so you get the exact metric on the train split, in seconds, on CPU.

## What is inside

- **local_score.py** the fork-magnet. `local_score("my_train_submission.csv", TRAIN_DIR)` returns the exact `score = adjusted_edge_jaccard + 0.1 * division_jaccard`, plus per-dataset rows. Reads each dataset's voxel scale from its metadata and drops dangling edges, exactly like the official evaluator.
- **tracking_cellmot/** the organisers' scoring package, vendored verbatim (three files, self-contained) under its own BSD 3-Clause LICENSE. Because this is their code and not a reimplementation, the number cannot drift from the leaderboard. Credit and copyright are theirs (github.com/royerlab/kaggle-cell-tracking-competition).
- **dataset_stats.csv** derived, aggregate summaries of the 199 train ground-truth graphs: node, edge and division counts, timepoints, voxel scale, the estimated true node count, and nodes per frame. This is where you see how sparsely the ground truth is labelled, which is why a clean prediction can score above 1.0.
- **make_stats.py** regenerates that table over any ground-truth directory.
- **metric_cheatsheet.md** the whole metric on one page, in plain words.
- **submission_template.csv** the exact submission row format, one node example and one edge example.

## Quick use, on Kaggle with internet on

```python
import numpy as np, subprocess, sys
NPV = np.__version__   # pin numpy so the install cannot break the image ABI
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "tracksdata==0.1.0rc6", "polars", "geff", f"numpy=={NPV}"])
import sys; sys.path.append("/kaggle/input/biohub-local-scoring-support-pack")
from local_score import local_score
TRAIN = "/kaggle/input/competitions/biohub-cell-tracking-during-development/train"
summary, rows = local_score("my_train_submission.csv", TRAIN)
print(summary["score"])
```

## Provenance and rules

Nothing here is competition data. The scorer is public BSD-3 source, the cheatsheet and glue are my own writing, `dataset_stats.csv` is transformative aggregate statistics (counts and medians, never coordinates or images), and the template is synthetic. Companion notebook that explains and demonstrates the scorer: [Score your cell tracker locally](https://www.kaggle.com/code/busyaprime/score-your-cell-tracker-locally).

info.title: Biohub Local CV Pack: Folds, GT Stats, Scorer
info.subtitle: Prefix-holdout folds, per-volume GT stats, scorer harness, board timeline
info.description:
# Biohub Local CV Pack: Folds, GT Stats, Scorer

Everything you need to validate a Biohub cell-tracking pipeline locally instead of reading the public leaderboard: a fixed two-fold prefix-holdout split over all 195 clean train volumes, per-volume ground-truth statistics, the local scoring harness for the competition's own `tracking_cellmot` metric, per-volume behavior of a public 0.915-class fork pipeline, and a dated public-leaderboard snapshot plus timeline showing why local validation is the only measurement that predicts anything.

## Why this exists

The four public test volumes of `biohub-cell-tracking-during-development` are train twins: `44b6_0113de3b`, `44b6_0b24845f`, `6bba_05b6850b`, `6bba_05db0fb1`. The public leaderboard therefore rewards memorization, ~243 teams share a displayed 0.915 from one fork lineage (ranks 332–574 on 2026-08-20 — entirely below the bronze line at rank 258, displayed 0.917), and Kaggle displays 3 decimals while ranking on full precision. A rank inside that block is a queue position, not a result. If you want a number that survives private scoring, you need local validation on volumes your pipeline has never seen — that is what this pack provides.

## Files

- `folds_prefix_holdout.csv` — the fold protocol, one row per clean train volume (195). Fold A tunes on the `6bba` family (n=126) and evaluates on `44b6` (n=69); fold B reverses. The four public-test twin volumes are already excluded from these tables (195 clean = 199 minus the 4 twins); the is_public_test_twin column is retained for anyone rebuilding with twins included.
- `gt_per_volume_stats.csv` — per-volume ground-truth statistics for all 195 volumes: annotated nodes/edges, metadata node-count estimate (`est`), frames spanned, nodes-per-frame level/dispersion/trend, division counts, and frame-to-frame displacement percentiles (`disp_med/p95/p99/max`, in anisotropy-scaled units, scale (1.625, 0.40625, 0.40625)). Use `disp_p99` for gating radii and `est` for node budgets.
- `fork162_per_volume_run_stats.csv` — per-volume pipeline telemetry (78 columns: node/edge counts, edge-to-node ratio, division-like sources, gap-closing and relink counters) from our measurement run of a recovered public 0.916-targeting fork variant across the same 195 volumes. Useful as a calibration reference for what a 0.915-class pipeline emits per volume.
- `public_leaderboard_2026-08-20.csv` — full 2,580-row public leaderboard snapshot (2026-08-20T20:16Z, Kaggle CLI): Rank, TeamId, TeamName, LastSubmissionDate, Score, SubmissionCount, TeamMemberUserNames.
- `leaderboard_timeline.csv` — dated reads of the 0.915 block's decay: a frozen fork entry fell rank 360 → 531 between 2026-08-19 and 2026-08-20 while its score never moved, and the bronze-line display crossed 0.916 → 0.917.
- `score.py`, `eval_setup.py`, `control.py` — the local scoring harness. Runs inside a Kaggle kernel with the competition attached: it locates the competition's own `tracking_cellmot` scorer under `/kaggle/input`, builds the prediction graph per volume, and reports per-volume and fold-level scores. `control.py` re-scores an unchanged reference alongside any candidate; require control drift 0.000000 before believing a delta.
- `build_pack.py` — deterministic builder for the derived CSVs in this pack.

## Method / provenance

All statistics were computed by us from the competition's train split (195 clean volumes; the 4 public twins excluded from every evaluation) using the fixed prefix-holdout protocol above, on the competition's own scorer. The fork telemetry comes from executing a publicly shared pipeline variant (pilkwang-lineage artifacts; the plain 0.915 fork's upstream source is no longer retrievable) through the same harness. Leaderboard files are unmodified Kaggle CLI downloads. Nothing here contains competition image data — only derived statistics, fold definitions, code, and public leaderboard records. Reference points measured with this exact harness: an honest from-scratch lane at CV 0.548526 scored 0.595 public; confirmed-on-both-folds steps included per-volume budget plus edgeless-node pruning (fold A 0.471149 -> 0.501604, fold B 0.495111 -> 0.580255) and sub-voxel refinement (CV 0.540929 -> 0.548526).

## Mount and use

```python
import pandas as pd
folds = pd.read_csv('/kaggle/input/biohub-local-cv-pack/folds_prefix_holdout.csv')
gt = pd.read_csv('/kaggle/input/biohub-local-cv-pack/gt_per_volume_stats.csv')
eval_A = folds[folds.fold_A_role == 'evaluate'].volume  # twins are already excluded from these tables
```

Companion notebook (walkthrough + what actually moves the metric): "Bronze moved to 0.917 — your 0.915 is sinking".

## Limitations

Ground-truth annotations in this competition are sparse, so `nodes` counts annotated cells, not all cells (`est` is the volume-metadata estimate of the full count). The fork telemetry describes one recovered variant, not the exact plain-0.915 checkpoint. Leaderboard files are point-in-time snapshots; re-pull for current standings.

## License and credit

CC0-1.0 for everything in this pack. The scorer it wraps (`tracking_cellmot`) ships with the competition and stays there — this pack contains only our wrapper code. Credit to `inversion`'s nearest-neighbor getting-started notebook, `pilkwang`'s public model/support artifacts, and `yusuketogashi`'s no-hack local-CV line for the public groundwork this builds on.

info.title: biohub-tracking-src
info.subtitle: Reusable Python package for 3D+time cell detection, tracking & submission
info.description:
# biohub-tracking-src

Source code (the `biohub_tracking` Python package) for a 3D+time cell-tracking
pipeline built for the **Biohub – Cell Tracking During Development** competition.
This dataset exists so the code can be imported inside a **Kaggle notebook with
internet disabled** — you attach it as an input and `import biohub_tracking`.

## Context
The competition asks you to detect cells in 3D microscopy volumes over time, link
them across frames, and reconstruct cell-division lineages, scored by edge Jaccard
+ 0.1 × division Jaccard. Voxels are anisotropic (z=1.625, y=x=0.40625 µm), labels
are sparse, and submission notebooks must run offline within 12 hours.
## What it does
A tracking-by-detection pipeline that keeps detection and linking as separate,
auditable stages, with every spatial decision made in physical (micron) space:
- **data/** – lazy Zarr volume reader (one timepoint at a time) + sparse `.geff`
  ground-truth graph reader + a metadata-only dataset probe.
- **geometry** – voxel↔micron conversion and anisotropy-aware distance/gating.
- **detect/** – classical local-maxima detector (no weights) and a 3D UNet heatmap
  detector trained from sparse point labels, with micron-unit non-max suppression.
- **link/** – physical-space Hungarian frame-to-frame linking into a lineage graph.
- **submit/** – streaming `submission.csv` writer (exact competition schema) and an
  end-to-end per-dataset pipeline (detect → link → write).
- **experiments/** – offline experiment registry (config, metrics, reproducibility
  lineage), plus resumable training with dataset caching, EDA reporting, and
  metric-progress plots.
## Why it's needed
Kaggle rerun notebooks have no internet, so custom code can't be `pip install`ed —
it must be attached as a dataset. This package lets a lightweight submission
notebook do inference only, producing a valid submission within the runtime limit,
while the (optional) trained weights are attached separately.
## How to reuse it
```python
import sys; 
# auto-locate the attached package
from pathlib import Path
src = next(Path('/kaggle/input').glob('**/biohub_tracking/__init__.py')).parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(src))
from biohub_tracking.submit.pipeline import run_submission, classical_detector
run_submission(
    test_dir='/kaggle/input/biohub-cell-tracking-during-development/test',
    out_path='/kaggle/working/submission.csv',
    detector=classical_detector(),   # or swap in a trained-model detector
)

info.title: biohub-cellmot-baseline
info.subtitle: Trained weights + patched code for the BioHub cell-tracking competition
info.description:
# Cell Tracking Baseline (UNet + Transformer)

A ready-to-run baseline for the [BioHub â€“ Cell Tracking During Development](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/biohub-cell-tracking-during-development) competition: cell detection and linking in 3D+time light-sheet microscopy with **sparse ground truth**. A short tracking demo (`assets/demo.gif`) and metric figures ship in the dataset files.

## What's inside

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `weights/baseline/split_0/edge_predictor_best.pth` | Trained joint detector + linker checkpoint (~8 MB). Same weights as the public [UNet baseline inference notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/thibautgoldsborough/unet-baseline-inference-submission); **not** trained to convergence â€” expect gains from training longer. |
| `weights/baseline/split_0/config.json` | Architecture config for the checkpoint (channels, layers, downsample, pool kernel). |
| `src/tracking_cellmot/` | Model definitions (`TemporalUNet3D`, `SimpleNodeTransformer`), the competition metric (`metrics.py`, `division_metrics.py`), and dataset IO. |
| `scripts/predict_unet_transformer.py` | Inference: detection + linking â†’ `.geff` graphs. Patched with `--edge-threshold`, `--pool-kernel-um`, `--max-children`, a split detection/linking path, and a parameter-free distance linker. |
| `scripts/linking.py` | Standalone linker: physical-distance gate, Hungarian assignment, constant-velocity motion model, single-frame gap closing. Pure array work, no GPU. |
| `scripts/train_unet_transformer.py` | Training with gate-aligned candidate sampling and `link_acc * test_recall` checkpoint selection. |
| `scripts/sweep_linkers.py`, `scripts/sweep_detection.py` | One detection pass per video, many linker / detector configs replayed on CPU. |
| `scripts/geffs_to_csv.py`, `scripts/csv_to_geffs.py` | Submission round-trip: `.geff` graphs â†” Kaggle submission CSV. |
| `scripts/evaluate.py` | Score predicted `.geff`s against ground-truth `.geff`s (no images loaded). |
| `tests/` | Metric unit tests and division sandbox examples. |
| `metrics.md` | The competition metric, explained with worked examples. |

## Quick start

```bash
uv sync
uv run python scripts/predict_unet_transformer.py --method baseline --split 0 \
  --edge-threshold 0.01 --pool-kernel-um 5.0 --max-children 1
uv run python scripts/evaluate.py \
  --pred-dir predictions/$USER/baseline/split_0 --gt-dir data/train
```

See `README.md` for the full training / prediction / submission workflow and the Python API.

## Gotchas worth knowing

- **Always pass `--edge-threshold` explicitly.** The upstream default (0.5) emits **zero edges** at inference density (~240 candidates/frame â†’ softmax â‰ˆ 0.004), and the metric then silently reports score `0.0` without running node matching.
- `--pool-kernel-um` quantises hard: it becomes `round(um / 1.625)` voxels forced odd, so 3.0 / 4.0 / 5.0 are all the same setting (kernel 3).
- Coordinates in the `.geff` files are **voxel indices** â€” scale by `(1.625, 0.40625, 0.40625)` Âµm/voxel before any distance reasoning.
- Score = `adjusted_edge_jaccard + 0.1 Ã— division_jaccard` â€” edges dominate 10:1.
- The classical-linker config above reaches roughly **0.74** on the public leaderboard; the neural edge score does not beat plain proximity once candidates are distance-gated.

## License

CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication). The checkpoint derives from the public competition baseline notebook; the metric and model code are the competition's provided baseline with local CLI patches.

info.subtitle: E.coli tracking - Graph Neural Network training dataset
info.description:
This is a dataset containing fluorescence time lapse images of E. coli cells (1 pixel = 0.11 mu), the corresponding cell information (lookup table), and the adjacency matrix. The data can be used for any tracking project.
 
This dataset was used to train a Graph Neural Network to track E.coli MG1655 cells in fluorescent time-lapse image stacks. For details see https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jpcb.4c02745

File format: npy
Each file contains:
images: numpy array (frames, height, width) uint16
look_up_table: numpy array (each row represent a cell width all its information in the current frame)
adjacency_matrix_gt: numpy array, this is a square array with dimensions length lookup table x length lookup table. Each row and column represents a cell in the lookup table.

The columns of the lookup table array:

tiff series (field of view tiff file)

ROI

frame

total number of cells in the ROI

cell number

bounding box centroid coordinate x

bounding box centroid coordinate y

bounding box min x coordinate

bounding box max x coordinate

bounding box min y coordinate

bounding box max y coordinate

cell centroid coordinate x

cell centroid coordinate y

cell width (in mu)

cell height (in mu)

cell angle (deg)

info.title: Fuse My Cells-Part-01
info.subtitle: Fuse My Cells: From Single View to Fused Multiview Lightsheet Imaging Challenge
info.description:
🔎 About¶
France-BioImaging's Fuse My Cells challenge aims to advance new methods for 3D image-to-image fusion using deep learning in the fields of biology and microscopy.

In multi-view microscopy, to create a fused 3D image stack, it is necessary to capture several views (typically from 2 to 4) of the sample from different angles and then align them in the same spatial reference frame to generate a 3D fusion of these images. The fused image compensates for point spread function anisotropy and signal degradation for acquisitions deep in the sample, at the expense of an increased photon exposition, damaging to the sample.

The main objective of the Fuse My Cells challenge is to predict a fused 3D image using only one 3D view, providing a practical solution to the limitations of current microscopy techniques, such as improving image quality, extending the duration of live imaging, saving on the photon budget, and facilitating image analysis.

🎯 Task
![](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F4678197%2F4b56befd53e769727eb2464835bb45e1%2Fimage_2025-01-27_121842688.png?generation=1737962323939768&alt=media)

💡 Context
🔬 Optical (photonic) microscopy is commonly used to image live organisms. However, its invasive nature can cause light-induced damage, such as photobleaching, where fluorophores lose their ability to emit light, and phototoxicity, which harms living cells. These problems are accentuated when imaging biological systems over long periods, as prolonged exposure can compromise both data accuracy and quality.

🔬 Confocal microscopy is widely used for high-resolution 3D imaging. Laser scanning confocal, spinning disk or Airy disk microscope allow for efficient z-sectioning (the ability to suppress fluorescence signal from outside the focal plane) and near diffraction limited resolution. Yet laser scanning excitation exposes the sample to a high photon flux. This makes long-term imaging of living cells a challenge for confocal microscopy, as the cumulative light exposure can negatively affect cell health and reduce image quality in prolonged experiments.

🔬 Lightsheet microscopy, such as Single Plane Illumination Microscopy (SPIM), is an alternative 3D microscopy technique that can overcome some of confocal microscopy's issues. In these microscopes, the excitation optical path is perpendicular with the detection axis, and aligned with the detection focal plane. Instead of a point detector, a full camera chip is used. This way only the plane of interest is illuminated at each acquisition. This reduces the total light exposure on the sample, saving on the photon budget. Furthermore, some SPIM setup allow imaging of samples usually bigger that classical inverted microscope statiffs. In particular the sample is usually hung in front of the detection objective, allowing it to rotate freely around the vertical axis.

However, despite these advantages, lightsheet microscopy still faces challenges, especially when imaging deep within a sample (beyond 100 µm). Similar to confocal microscopy, lightsheet techniques suffer from a degradation in their point spread function (PSF) —the microscope’s response to a point source—, meaning the resolution is higher laterally (in the camera focal plane) than axially (along the detection optical axis). As the imaging depth increases, the PSF degrades, and the signal-to-background ratio decreases, leading to a loss in image quality. Thus, larger samples, such as embryos, can pose challenges for uniform illumination and resolution across the entire volume, while optical aberrations, like astigmatism, may affect the clarity of the images, especially when attempting to capture fine 3D details.

🔬 A solution to these limitations is multiview lightsheet microscopy associated with multiview fusion imaging. This approach improves 3D resolution by combining multiple views of the sample from different acquired angles, resulting in higher quality images with less distortion and shadowing, and facilitating subsequent analyses such as segmentation, tracking and quantification of biological structures.

However, multiview lightsheet microscopy introduces additional complexities: sample preparation is more complex and the photon budget is distributed across all angles, all channels and all over time: all of these can also lead to photobleaching and phototoxicity. Then, imaging living cells becomes a challenge, because, the more time goes by, the more photons the sample collects, and the less photon budget remains for following time periods, all divided for each view and for each channel.

✨ Our solution: Fuse My Cells Challenge
![](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-user-content/o/inbox%2F4678197%2Ffcbd087aaf91f7f925e52c824e877240%2Fimage_2025-01-27_121919451.png?generation=1737962360805577&alt=media)

The Fuse My Cells France-Bioimaging Challenge proposes a solution : to construct a comprehensive database that empowers competitors to develop methods for predicting fused multiview 3D images from only a single view.

These methods will not only retain all the advantages of multi-view light sheet microscopy, but also minimize the need for additional views and save photon budgets. This will open up new possibilities in imaging experiments, such as adding new fluorescent channels, extending the duration of live imaging, or exploring more complex studies with reduced chance of photobleaching or phototoxicity.

After a first challenge – Light My Cells presented at ISBI 2024 in Athens –, the second France BioImaging challenge, Fuse My Cells, ultimate goal is to produce robust and open-source methods capable of handling the large variability in biological imaging data. We build the extensive database thanks to the structuration role of the France-Bioimaging national infrastructure which federates 23 imaging sites across France.



🚀 Prospectives
If successful, the Fuse My Cells challenge can lead to robust methods for image deep learning fusion processing. Then, it will be possible to use deep learning methods such as domain adaptation or transfer learning to apply these techniques to other microscope setups or modalities without multiview capabilities. This would result in better imaging quality and 3D resolution which will be able to improve segmentation, tracking, fewer artifacts and expanding the potential for biological imaging across different platforms and experimental setups.
